extracted.subtask_description: Recommended Marking Scheme for the 32nd United States of America Mathematical Olympiad (May 1, 2003). Specifies scoring philosophy, allowed point allocations and detailed point-by-point credit guidance for each of the six problems and their solution approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: General grading philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The general philosophy of this marking scheme follows that of IMO 2002. This scheme encourages complete solutions. Partial credits will be given under more strict circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each solution shall be graded from one of two approaches: (1) from 7 going down (a complete solution with possible minor errors); (2) from 0 going up (a solution missing at least one critical idea). Most partial credits are not additive. Graders are encouraged to choose the approach most favorable to students, but partial credits from different approaches are not additive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two grading approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Each solution by students shall be graded from one of the two approaches: (1) from 7 going down; (2) from 0 going up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach (1) assumes a complete solution with possible minor errors (start at 7 and deduct). Approach (2) constructs score from 0 upward for solutions missing at least one critical idea. Do not mix partial credits across approaches (partial credits from different approaches are not additive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial credits non-additivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Most partial credits are not additive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple partial steps from different approaches are present, graders should not simply sum point suggestions from different approaches; follow the stated additive rules per problem (examples like '1+2=2', '1+1+2=2' given in various problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grader latitude to choose approach favorable to student
rubrics_metrics.description: Graders are encouraged to choose the approach that most favorable to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a problem admits multiple solution approaches, graders may assess the student's work according to the approach that yields the most favorable (but fair) credit, subject to non-additivity rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 1: induction setup credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for setting up clear induction steps and making attempts to discuss numbers N1, N2, N3, N4, N5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when the student correctly sets up the induction and considers the five candidate numbers; partial or unclear setups may get reduced credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 1: completion credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 points for completing the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full completion of the inductive argument showing one of N1..N5 divisible by 5^{n+1} and concluding the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 1: 'induction' mention penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: No points should be given for just mentioning induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the student merely writes 'by induction' without any supporting argument, give 0. If inductive step arguments are unclear, deduct 2 points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 1: allowed scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible marks for this problem are 0, 2, 5, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed discrete score options when combining partial credit (do not invent intermediate totals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 2: reduction to quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for reducing this problem to a problem on convex quadrilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when the student correctly reduces the general polygon dissection problem to proving the lemma for convex quadrilaterals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (first approach): coordinate setup credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for setting up coordinates and verifying the rationality of at least one non-trivial component of a vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student places A=(0,0), C=(c,0), sets B=(a,b), D=(d,e) and shows some coordinate (e.g., a or d) is rational using the given rational distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (first approach): AP rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: 4 points for showing one of AP, BP, CP, DP are rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student computes coordinates for intersection P and shows e.g. AP is rational via algebraic expressions derived from rational side/diagonal lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (first approach): additive rule and possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: As in the first approach, 1+2 = 2 rule applies here. The possible marks following this approach are 0, 1, 2, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial credits combine according to provided small-sum rules (e.g., do not sum 1 and 2 to get 3; 1+2 counts as 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2 (second approach): proving Lemma 2
rubrics_metrics.description: 4 points for proving Lemma 2 (about rational cosines and equivalence of angles). 2 points can be given for failed attempts with decent arguments on rationalities of cosine values with correct cosine and sine addition formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award full credit for complete proof of parts (a),(b),(c); partial credit for substantial but incomplete attempts using correct identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (second approach): use of Law of Sines finishing touch
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for final step applying Law of Sines to deduce AP and BP (and similarly CP, DP) have rational lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student uses equivalence of angles and Law of Sines to conclude rational segment lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (second approach): additional partial-credit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: Without a complete proof of Lemma 2, there will be at most 2 points given. After proving Lemma 2, we require students to have at least 2 of remaining subtle parts to obtain more partial credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce thresholding: proving Lemma 2 is necessary to obtain significant credit in this approach; combine later-part credits only as allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (second approach): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible marks following this approach are 0, 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 (even though a score of 5 is very unlikely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the discrete allowed scores when assigning total for this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (third approach): proof that sin A1 sin A2 is rational
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for proving sin A1 sin A2 is rational (from cosine rationalities and addition formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student deduces product of sines is rational using cosine data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (third approach): ratio of sines rational
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for showing sin A2 / sin A1 is rational (manipulation leading to ratio being rational).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student gives algebraic manipulation to obtain rational ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (third approach): area/ratio implication to PD/BP
rubrics_metrics.description: 4 points for proving from area ratios that BP/PD is rational and concluding AP, PC rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student uses area ratios, Law of Cosines input, and rationality of sine ratios to deduce segment rationality; note combinatorial partial-credit rules (1+1+1 = 2 etc.) as given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (third approach): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible marks following this approach are 0, 1, 2, 6, 7 (scores like 5 unlikely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow discrete allowed totals for this approach; respect stated additive rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3 / fourth approach: linear system reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for reducing to a linear system: writing projection equations c1 x + c2 z = c, c4 y + c3 z = a and eliminating z to get rational linear relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student derives the 2×2 linear system relating x,y and shows coefficients are rational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3 / fourth approach: determinant nonzero case
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for solving the system when determinant c1 c3 + c2 c4 ≠ 0 and concluding x,y rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award for solving and concluding x,y rational in non-degenerate case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3 / fourth approach: determinant zero impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points (included in above) / reasoning that determinant vanishing leads to impossible geometric configuration; conclude determinant ≠ 0 and hence x,y rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student shows cos φ1 cos φ3 = − cos φ2 cos φ4 leads to contradiction with convexity etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (fourth approach): final finishing touch
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for final step: applying lemma to triangles to obtain BP, DP, AP, CP rational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student connects lemma conclusions to original quadrilateral to finish proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (fourth approach): additive rules and possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: 1+1 = 1, 1+2 = 2, 1+1+2 = 2. Partial credits are additive with complete proof of Lemma 3. Possible marks: 0,1,2,5,6,7 (score 5 unlikely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the explicit small-sum combination rules for partial credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 2: caution about 4×4 projection system
rubrics_metrics.description: Note explaining a pitfall: projecting intersection O onto four side lines yields a 4×4 linear system; conclusion of rationality via Cramer's rule only valid if determinant ≠ 0; determinant may vanish in some configurations (e.g., rectangles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not award credit that incorrectly uses a vanishing-determinant argument; emphasize need for Lemma 2 in many configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 2: overall possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the various approaches of Problem 2, many specific possible mark sets are listed per approach; ensure to use the appropriate set per approach (examples: 0,1,2,7; 0,1,2,4,6,7; 0,1,2,5,6,7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign final score for Problem 2 according to the approach used and its listed possible totals; do not mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 3: proving ai ≤ t(ai)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for stating and proving ai ≤ t(ai) for i=0,...,n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student shows any ai > 0 is preceded by at least ai distinct values different from ai, so t(ai) ≥ ai.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 3: stabilization after finitely many t
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for stating and proving that index-bounded sequences stabilize after finitely many applications of t and that once ai = t(ai) it remains unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student proves monotonicity, boundedness, and permanence properties leading to finite stabilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 3: induction to n−1 applications
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for the inductive argument showing no more than n applications of t are needed (and concluding at most n−1 for n+1-term sequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student correctly performs induction base and step controlling behavior of index n+1 term and uses stabilization of subsequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 3: possible marks and remark
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: The possible marks for this problem are 0, 1, 4, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed discrete totals; do not award partial sums outside this set unless justified by scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4 (first solution): construction credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for constructing G (extend DM through M so that FG ∥ CD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student identifies and constructs parallelogram/point G as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4 (first solution): reduction to angle information
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for reducing side equality MC = MF to an equivalent angle condition (e.g., ∠GCD = ∠FDA leading to cyclic/quadrilateral equivalence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student correctly translates segment equality to cyclicity/angle equalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4 (first solution): completing the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: 5 points for completing the proof that MC = MF ⇔ MB·MD = MC^2 using similarity and cyclic quadrilateral arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award full credit for correct chain of equivalences through similarity and algebraic conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4 (first solution): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible marks for this problem are 0, 1, 2, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow provided discrete totals; partial results without final connection limited to small scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4 (second solution): partial credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed point assignments: 1 point for proving MB·MD = MC^2 ⇒ MF = MC fact about similar triangles; 2 points for next part; 2 points for Ceva-related step; 2 points for final deductions; 3 points for proving MB·MD = MC^2 implying MF = MC; 4 points for reverse implication MF = MC ⇒ MB·MD = MC^2. Two partial credits from different parts are not additive; a partial credit in one part and a full mark in the other are not additive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use given split and non-additivity rules when awarding credits for second solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4: overall partial-credit non-additivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Two partial credits from different parts are not additive. A partial credit in one part and a full mark in the other are not additive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce constraints so final score for this problem follows allowed aggregates in scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 4: allowed totals reminder
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible marks are 0,1,2,3,4,7 depending on which parts are completed (3 only for first part etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to enumerated allowed totals for this problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (first solution): homogeneity and reduction credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for homogeneous approach and expressing b + c in terms of a (rescaling to a + b + c = 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student recognizes homogeneity and reduces variables appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (first solution): completion credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 6 points for completing the proof (manipulations of f(x) and bound f(a)+f(b)+f(c) ≤ 8). No partial credits given in this part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award full credit only for a correct complete derivation; otherwise 0 for this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (first solution): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The possible marks for this approach are 0, 1, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these discrete outcomes for first solution approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (second solution): transform to sum-of-squares form
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for transforming the inequality into equivalent form involving (a−b−c)^2/(2a^2+(b+c)^2) etc., and reducing to inequality (1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student performs algebraic manipulations to obtain sum-of-squares inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (second solution): final inequality step
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for completing the final algebraic deduction that LHS ≥ 1/2 by expanding and relating to sum of squares (equivalently showing (a−b)^2+(b−c)^2+(c−a)^2 ≥ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student shows equivalence and concludes inequality with equality case a=b=c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (second solution): partial-credit guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: 3 points for reducing to inequality (1). 1 point for a serious but unsuccessful attempt to use a and b + c as two variables will be awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide small credit for reasonable but incomplete attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (second solution): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible marks for this approach are 0, 1, 3, 6, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to allowed totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (third solution): cyclic-sum transformation credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for transforming into the cyclic sum form (equation (2)) and factoring numerator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student converts inequality into cyclic-sum expression and recognizes factorization (2a−x)(2a−5x) etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (third solution): inequality manipulation credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 6 points for deriving inequality (3) and completing the argument that final inequality follows (showing (2a−x)^2(5a+x) ≥ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student proves the needed intermediate inequality and concludes equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (third solution): possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible marks for this approach are 0, 1, 7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use listed totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 5 (fourth solution): symmetric-sum / Schur / AM-GM steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Point breakdown: 1 point for multiplying out correctly; 3 points for proving an inequality derived from Schur; 1 point for an AM-GM based inequality; 2 points for a further symmetric inequality; adding these yields final result. Partial credits additive rules given: 1+1=2 and others; possible marks 0,1,2,3,7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award points for each algebraic inequality piece if correctly stated and proved; combine according to additive rules described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: overall strategy claim credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for claiming: from any position with odd sum it is possible to reach the all-zero position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student formulates the main reachability claim as starting point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: two-step strategy formulation credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for outlining the two-step strategy: (a) from odd-sum move to exactly one odd number; (b) from exactly one odd number move to an odd sum with strictly smaller maximum or to all-zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when both steps are clearly stated as the plan to reach all-zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: step (a) parity manipulations credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for proving step (a): given odd sum, show how to reach position with exactly one odd number using parity move sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student demonstrates parity sequences that transform triples A,C,E or B,D,F as described to one odd entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: step (b) maximum-decreasing argument credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for proving step (b): from configuration with exactly one odd number, produce moves that either decrease the maximum while keeping sum odd or reach the all-zero position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student presents case analysis for M even/odd and shows sequences that reduce maximum or reach zero; includes sub-cases C>0, E>0, C=E=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: combining partial credits rule for this problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial credits are not additive. 1 point will be rewarded for somewhat applying a maximum value argument. 3 points will be awarded for stating the strategies clearly and carrying out significant progress; in other words, 2+2 = 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining evidence of progress, use the specified compression of summed partials (e.g., two 2-point contributions may yield total 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: possible marks for first solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible marks for this approach are 0, 1, 2, 3, 6/7. (6 points for near-perfect combinatorial argument; 5 very unlikely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign final score respecting these listed totals and the non-linear add rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6 (second solution): small claims credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for claiming: if there is a pair of opposite vertices with odd sum, we can reduce to all-zero position. 1 point for focusing on such pair with minimal possible max(a,d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student states and motivates reduction to smallest-opposite-pair strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6 (second solution): alternate-updating and cycle analysis credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 point for applying alternate-update process to arc and showing eventual control of max(x,y); 2 points for proving the arc enters a unique 4-cycle modulo 2 and each parity occurs equally often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student analyzes the modulo-2 cycles and uses them to bound values and construct desired configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6 (second solution): final configuration and finishing moves credit
rubrics_metrics.description: 2 points for assembling both arcs and showing one can reach position with specified xi properties and then performing moves to reach all-zero position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award when student completes the reduction to (a,a,a,a,a,0) or equivalent and executes finishing sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6 (second solution): additive rules and possible marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: For this approach 1+1=2, 1+1+1=2, 1+2=2, 1+1+2=1+1+1+2=3. Possible marks: 0,1,2,3,6/7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the given combination rules when totaling partial credits in this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 6: note on invariant and gcd scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: Positions of the form 0 1 1 1 1 0 (mod 2) and rotations cannot reach all-zero because moves preserve parity pattern; dividing out gcd of six numbers doesn't affect reachability, so assume numbers not all even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not award solutions that ignore parity obstruction; check gcd/scale invariance when analyzing reachability.
